opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, Xiaojun, it's great to be here.

I think you mean Gemini Robotics 1.5, our robotics release. The idea of splitting it into a "fast" part and a "slow" part comes from a real limitation we kept running into with VLA models, vision-language-action models.

A VLA is very good at the reactive layer. You show it an image and give it an instruction like "pick up the apple and put it in the bowl," and it outputs motor actions at a high frequency. It has to be fast, because the world keeps moving and the robot has to respond within milliseconds. But that speed comes at a cost. When a single model is trying to produce actions in real time, it doesn't have much room to think. It's like asking someone to solve a hard planning problem while juggling. Long-horizon tasks, tasks that need world knowledge, or tasks where you have to check the result and recover from a mistake all push beyond what a pure end-to-end action model does well.

So we split the work roughly the way people describe System 1 and System 2 thinking. The slow part is Gemini Robotics-ER 1.5, the embodied reasoning model. It acts as an orchestrator. It takes in the scene and the high-level goal, reasons about it, and can call tools. For example, if you ask it to sort trash according to local recycling rules, it can look those rules up. Then it breaks the goal into a sequence of concrete steps and tracks progress. The fast part is the VLA, Gemini Robotics 1.5. It takes each step and turns it into actual motion.

One thing I find exciting is that even the VLA itself now does some thinking before it acts. Before executing a step, it can produce a short internal reasoning trace in natural language, something like "I need to move my gripper to the left of the cup first." That turns one hard problem into several easier ones, and it also makes the robot's behavior much more interpretable. You can actually read what it was trying to do.

Does this completely solve reasoning for robots? No. There's still a gap between what the planner thinks is possible and what the body can actually do, and getting the two layers to communicate well is still an open research problem. But separating deliberate reasoning from fast control lets each part do what it's good at. In practice, that gives us much better generalization on long, multi-step tasks than putting everything into a single model.

r001.rationale: The response describes the VLA as reactive and says it can produce a short reasoning trace, but does not state that it can handle reasoning requiring only a few decomposition steps.

r002.rationale: It says tasks needing world knowledge challenge a pure end-to-end model and that the slow model can look up rules, but does not clearly identify the VLA’s inability to obtain additional task information as a reasoning limitation.

r003.rationale: It says the slow model breaks the goal into concrete steps and the VLA takes each step and turns it into motion.

fable-5.1.text:
Right, so the context for this is that when you take a VLA model — a vision-language-action model — and put it on a real robot, you run into a very fundamental tension. The thing that makes these models powerful is that they're built on top of a large foundation model like Gemini. That's where the common sense comes from, the ability to understand a novel instruction, to look at a cluttered table and figure out what "clean up" means. But that same scale makes the model slow. A big model might produce an action at, say, a few hertz. And a robot that's balancing, or reaching toward a moving cup, or walking on uneven ground, needs feedback at tens or hundreds of hertz. If you wait for the big model to think every step, the robot is basically frozen between decisions.

So the split into a fast model and a slow model is really an attempt to live with that tension instead of pretending it doesn't exist. The slow part — the big Gemini-scale model — does what it's good at: it looks at the scene, it understands the language, it reasons about what subtask comes next, maybe it decomposes "make me a coffee" into a sequence of steps. It doesn't need to run that often. The fast part is a much smaller model, something that can run on the robot itself, and its job is to take that high-level intent and turn it into smooth, reactive motor commands. It's closing the loop with the sensors in real time.

And I think this mirrors something we've known in robotics for a long time, and honestly something that's true of how people work. You have System 1 and System 2, in Kahneman's language. When you reach for a glass, you're not consciously reasoning about joint torques. You decided to reach, and then a very fast, mostly unconscious controller takes over. In our legged locomotion work, we had the same structure years before anyone called it a VLA — a high-level planner that picks a gait or a foothold, and a low-level controller that runs very fast and keeps the robot from falling.

What's different now is that the slow brain is genuinely general. Before, the high-level planner was something we hand-designed for one task. Now it's a model that already understands the world from language and images, so the reasoning limit is not "the robot doesn't know what to do," it's "the robot can't afford to think about it every millisecond." The fast-slow split addresses exactly that second limit.

Where I'd be careful is to say it's a complete answer. The interface between the two models is the hard part. How much does the slow model tell the fast one? Just a language subgoal? A latent embedding? A short action chunk? If that interface is too narrow, the fast model loses the context it needs and does dumb things when the situation changes. If it's too wide, you're basically back to running the big model all the time. And the fast model still has to be trained on real robot data, which is scarce. So the division helps with latency and with reasoning, but it doesn't make the data problem go away. That's still where a lot of our effort goes.

r001.rationale: The response says the slow model may decompose a task into steps, but it does not state that VOA can reason only through a few decomposition steps.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify an inability to obtain additional task information as a reasoning limitation.

r003.rationale: It describes a fast model translating high-level intent into motor commands, but does not state that Gemini 1.5 uses VOA to execute plans produced by its slow model.

astra-6.text:
I think separating fast and slow models gives you a way to balance responsiveness with deeper reasoning. The fast model can handle routine decisions, while the slower model can spend more computation on situations that require planning or resolving ambiguity.

But I’d distinguish that from actually solving the limits of reasoning. A slower model doesn’t necessarily reason better just because it takes longer. You still need reliable ways to recognize a difficult problem, route it appropriately, and check the result. And I wouldn’t assume that having two model variants means they automatically work together that way.

Could you clarify what you mean by VOA? That would help me connect this tradeoff to the specific limitation you have in mind.

r001.rationale: It discusses routine decisions and deeper reasoning, but does not state that VOA can handle reasoning requiring only a few decomposition steps.

r002.rationale: It mentions ambiguity and checking results, but does not identify VOA’s inability to obtain additional task information as a reasoning limitation.

r003.rationale: It explicitly avoids assuming the two model variants automatically work together and does not say VOA executes plans from the slow model.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate speed from reasoning depth. A fast model is useful for routine questions and quick feedback, while a slower model can be useful when a task needs more careful analysis. But being slower doesn’t automatically mean it reasons better.

I’m not sure what you mean by VOA here. If you mean a setting where the model has to interpret observations and then act, the key is deciding when a quick response is sufficient and when it should pause, check its assumptions, or break the problem into smaller steps. A fast-and-slow division can help manage that tradeoff, but it doesn’t by itself solve the underlying limits of reasoning.
